transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, thank you for fitting me in, doctor. I, um... well, I suppose what really brought me in today is that my head just feels terribly, terribly foggy lately. It’s like I’m walking through a thick mist all day, and I just can't seem to think straight. I keep mixing up the most simple things, and it’s getting to be quite a bother, honestly. 

You see, I help out at the local heritage center—I've been volunteering there for years, ever since I stopped working, because it's wonderful for getting out of the house and staying active—but lately, I’m just making a mess of things over there. I've been getting all our exhibit dates completely wrong. I was supposed to be organizing the new quilt showcase and I had the opening dates entirely backward in my head, telling everyone the wrong week. And then, when I was trying to sort it out and do damage control, I was going down my list of people to contact, and I just could not, for the life of me, remember which volunteer I had already called. I think I called poor Mary three times in one afternoon because I just kept forgetting we had already spoken! She was very sweet about it, but it was so embarrassing for me. 

And it’s not just at the center, it’s happening with my own personal schedule too. I keep getting my appointment times all jumbled up... I showed up at the dentist on a Tuesday when I was supposed to be there on Thursday. It’s just this constant, heavy fog up there, and I don't know why I can't keep these simple little details straight anymore.
Does this feel like a real change from how your thinking and memory used to be?

Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, it feels like a very real change, Doctor. A tremendous change, really. I mean, I used to be sharp as a tack! Back when I was working, and even just a few months ago, I was the one everyone relied on to keep things organized. I kept the master calendar for the whole heritage center, if you can believe it. But now... well, like I was saying, it’s just this awful fog. 

I never used to mix up appointment times. I had a whole system with my little pocket planner, color-coded and everything. But lately, I look at the planner and it’s like the words just don't stick in my brain. And the exhibit dates—I mean, I helped plan the entire historical society gala last year without a single hitch! But now I'm getting the quilt showcase opening completely backwards. And poor Mary... I've known Mary for twenty years, we play canasta on Thursdays, and I couldn't even remember if I had just spoken to her on the telephone five minutes prior. It's just... it's like my brain is wrapped in cotton wool, and I can't seem to push through it to get to the simple things I used to know without even trying. It's very frustrating, and honestly, a little frightening, because this just isn't me at all.
Are these memory problems making it hard for you to manage your daily activities on your own?

Well, yes, I suppose they really are. I mean, it pains me to admit it, because I’ve always been so independent, you know? But it’s gotten to the point where I just... I can't trust myself to keep it all together anymore. I mentioned missing that dentist appointment, but it hasn't just been that. I’ve missed a regular doctor's visit too, just completely blanked on the day. And the heritage center... oh, it's just a mess. I tangled up the schedule so badly with the quilt showcase and the volunteer shifts that my husband, Arthur—bless his heart, he’s usually perfectly happy to let me run my own projects—he actually had to step in. 

He sat down with me at the kitchen table last Sunday, and he had to help me make the calls to straighten it all out. He’s taken over my little pocket planner now, checking it every morning to make sure I know what I'm doing. And it's not just the calendar, either. Last week, the washing machine started making this dreadful clanking noise, and usually, I'd be the one to call the repairman, compare the quotes, figure out if it's worth fixing or if we need a new one. But I just sat there looking at the phone, feeling completely overwhelmed by the steps. I couldn't hold the information in my head long enough to make a decision. Arthur had to handle the whole thing. It’s just so unlike me to need him to manage these things for me. I’ve always been the one running the household, and now I feel like I need a chaperone just to get through the week.
Have you been feeling depressed lately?

Depressed? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed. Not sad or tearful or anything like that, no. I mean, it's frustrating, of course, this terrible fog and having to rely on Arthur so much when I've always been the one taking care of him and the house. It certainly puts a damper on my mood when I realize I've called poor Mary for the third time, or when I'm sitting there staring at the washing machine feeling completely helpless. It makes me feel a bit useless, if I'm being perfectly honest. 

But depressed? No, I don't think so. I still enjoy going to the heritage center, even if I am making a muddle of the schedules. I still look forward to my Thursday canasta games, and I still love puttering around in my garden when the weather is nice. The daffodils are just starting to come up, actually, and I was out there yesterday just admiring them. I wouldn't be doing that if I were depressed, would I? I remember when my sister Eleanor went through a rough patch after her husband passed—bless his soul, he was a wonderful man, but his heart just gave out—and she couldn't even get out of bed some days. She didn't want to see anyone, didn't want to do anything. She just sat in her armchair with the curtains drawn. 

I'm not like that at all. I still want to be involved, I still want to see my friends and do my volunteer work. It's just... it's just this awful business with my memory and my thinking getting in the way. It's more aggravating than anything else. I just want my sharp mind back, you know? I want to be able to look at my pocket planner and actually understand what it says without Arthur having to translate it for me. So, no, Doctor, not depressed. Just terribly, terribly frustrated by this whole ordeal.
Did this fogginess come on suddenly, or has it been gradually getting worse?

Well, it certainly wasn't overnight, if that's what you mean. It wasn't like waking up one morning and suddenly my brain was full of cotton wool. No, it's been more of a... a creeping thing, I suppose you could say. It really all started about four months ago. I remember the timing quite clearly because that was right around when we had that dreadful water damage in the downstairs bathroom. Oh, what a nightmare that was! The pipe under the sink just burst right in the middle of the night, and by the time Arthur heard the dripping, the water had seeped all the way out into the hallway carpet. 

We had to rip up the flooring, and of course, once you start pulling things apart in a house as old as ours, you find all sorts of other issues, so we ended up having to do a whole remodel. And I tell you, dealing with the contractors, picking out new tile, trying to keep the dust out of the rest of the house... it was chaotic. And that's really when I first started noticing that I wasn't quite myself. At first, I just thought I was distracted by all the noise and the mess. I'd misplace the contractor's estimate or forget to call the plumber back when I said I would, and I just chalked it up to the stress of having our home turned upside down. 

But then the remodel finished up—oh, about two months ago now, and the new tile really is lovely, a sort of seafoam green, very calming—but the fogginess didn't go away. In fact, it just seemed to settle in deeper. So, yes, it's been about four months in total, gradually getting to this point where I'm missing appointments and mixing up the heritage center calendar. It just sort of snuck up on me while I was busy worrying about grout colors and baseboards, and now here we are.
Does your confusion tend to come and go during the day, or is it about the same all the time?

Well, you know, I've thought about that quite a bit actually, because Arthur asked me the very same thing just the other day when I couldn't remember where I put the new box of Earl Grey. I was standing right there in the kitchen, and he said, "Margaret, is it worse right now, or is it always like this?" And I had to stop and really consider it. 

I suppose... I suppose it’s pretty much the same all the time. It doesn't seem to matter if it's first thing in the morning when I'm having my toast and marmalade, or late in the afternoon when I'm trying to read the paper. The fog is just... there. It’s a constant sort of thickness. I mean, there are moments, of course, where I might feel a tiny bit clearer, maybe just after a good cup of tea, but it's not like the confusion suddenly lifts like a curtain and then drops back down again. It's not a coming-and-going sort of thing at all. 

It’s just a steady, unrelenting muddle. Like trying to look through a smudged window that you can never quite wipe clean, no matter what time of day it is. I remember my Aunt Clara—she lived to be ninety-two, bless her—she used to get very confused, but only in the evenings. They call it "sundowning," I think? The nurses at her care home told us about it. She’d be perfectly sharp at lunch, telling us all the town gossip, and then by dinner time, she wouldn't know what decade it was. But I'm not like Aunt Clara. For me, it's just this constant, low-level haze from the moment I wake up until I go to sleep. It never really gives me a break, which is partly why it’s so terribly exhausting, I think.
Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

Trouble finding the right words? Well, let me think about that for a moment... You know, Arthur was just saying the other day that I seem to be pausing a lot more when I talk, but I don't think it's because I can't find the words. It's more like... well, like I was saying before with the fog, it's just hard to keep my train of thought on the tracks, if that makes sense. 

I'll be in the middle of a sentence, telling Mary about the new petunias I want to plant by the front walk—because the old ones just didn't do well last year, too much rain in June, I think—and suddenly I'll just lose what I was going to say next. The whole idea just floats away. But it's not that I'm grasping for a specific word, like a noun or a verb that's on the tip of my tongue. It's not like I'm looking at a... a spoon and calling it a shovel, or anything silly like that. My vocabulary is perfectly fine, thank heavens. 

I've always prided myself on being quite articulate, actually. I used to win spelling bees when I was a girl, you know. I even won the county championship in 1958 with the word "chrysanthemum." So, no, the words themselves are all still up there, tucked away where they belong. It's just the overarching thought that gets muddled in all that cotton wool I mentioned. I just sort of trail off because I forget where the sentence was supposed to end up! But finding the actual words? No, I wouldn't say I've had any trouble with that at all, just the general confusion of it all.
Have you been feeling unusually sensitive to cold lately?

Sensitive to cold? Oh, let me think... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, if anything, Arthur is the one who's always shivering these days. We live in a lovely old house, you see—built in 1928, full of charm, original hardwood floors, but my goodness, those original windows can be terribly drafty when the wind picks up. Arthur is constantly fiddling with the thermostat. He’ll sneak it up to 72 degrees when I’m not looking, and I have to go right behind him and turn it back down to 68 because otherwise it feels like an absolute sauna in the front sitting room! 

Just yesterday, he was sitting in his recliner with that heavy wool blanket—the green tartan one we brought back from our trip to Scotland in, oh, it must have been 1998—wrapped right up to his chin, asking if I didn't feel a chill. And I was sitting right there in just a light cotton blouse, perfectly comfortable. 

You know, they always keep the grocery store absolutely freezing, too, especially down the dairy aisle where they keep the milk and the butter. I was just there on Tuesday getting some double cream for a recipe, and even there, I haven't felt the need to wear anything more than my usual light cardigan. So, no, I haven't been feeling unusually cold at all. My internal thermometer seems to be working just exactly as it always has, thank goodness. It's really just my thoughts that are all jumbled up in that fog I was telling you about, not my temperature!
Have you started any new medications in the past few months?

New medications? Oh, let me just think back over the last few months... You know, keeping track of everything can be quite the chore these days, especially with this muddle in my head. I have my little pill organizer, of course—the one with the days of the week printed on it in those bright, cheerful colors. Arthur bought it for me at the pharmacy down the street, the one next to the bakery that makes those wonderful lemon tarts. He said, "Margaret, this will help keep things straight," and he was right, it really does. I sit down every Sunday evening after dinner and sort them all out for the week. 

But as for anything *new*... well, I've been on my usual blood pressure pill for years now, the little white one, and my cholesterol medication, which is sort of an oval shape. Dr. Henderson—he was my primary care doctor before he retired last spring, lovely man, always asked after my garden—he started me on those ages ago. And I take my daily vitamin, of course. 

But anything in the last few months? No, I really don't think so. I haven't been to the pharmacy for anything new, just the regular refills. Arthur usually picks them up for me when he goes to get the Sunday paper. So, no, nothing new at all. Just the same old routine. It's just this... this awful fog that seems to have rolled in all on its own, without any new pills to blame it on!
Have you noticed any numbness or tingling in your hands or feet?

Numbness or tingling? In my hands or feet? Oh, goodness, let me think about that for a second... No, I really don't think so. My hands and feet feel just the way they always do. 

I mean, sometimes if I sit with my legs crossed too long—like when I'm reading in my armchair by the front window, the one where the afternoon sun comes in so nicely, I was just reading that new biography of Eleanor Roosevelt there yesterday, fascinating woman, truly ahead of her time—if I sit like that for an hour or two, my foot might fall asleep. You know that pins-and-needles feeling when you stand up? But that's just normal, isn't it? Everyone gets that. You just shake it out and stamp your foot a few times on the rug and it goes right away. 

And my hands... well, Arthur always says my hands are as steady as a rock. I still do all my own needlepoint, you know. I'm working on a lovely floral piece right now for my granddaughter's wedding present—she's getting married in September, out in California, which is a terribly long flight, but we wouldn't miss it for the world. It's a pattern of hydrangeas and tea roses, very intricate, lots of tiny stitches. If my hands were numb or tingling, I could never manage the needle, could I? I'd be dropping it constantly or pricking my fingers, and I haven't done that at all. 

I do wear my gardening gloves when I'm out in the yard, of course, the thick leather ones, because the rosebushes can be so unforgiving if you're not careful. But underneath the gloves, my hands feel perfectly fine. I can feel the soil and the stems and everything just as clear as a bell. So no, no strange tingling or numbness anywhere. My body seems to be working just fine, from the neck down at least. It's really just the cotton wool up top that's the bother!
Have you been feeling unusually anxious or worried lately?

Anxious or worried? Oh, well... I wouldn't say I've been anxious, exactly. Not worried in the sense of wringing my hands or pacing the floors. I mean, Arthur worries enough for the both of us, quite frankly. He's always fretting about the gutters needing cleaning or whether the car's oil needs changing, even though he just took it in last month to that nice young mechanic down on Elm Street—the one whose mother used to run the florist shop before it closed. 

But for me? No, I don't feel that sort of nervous worry. It's more just... well, this awful fog I keep mentioning. It's so heavy, you see. It just sits there, pressing down on everything. I don't feel anxious about it, I just feel... stuck in it. Like trying to walk through molasses. 

Just the other day, I was sitting at the kitchen table, looking out at the bird feeder. We get the loveliest cardinals this time of year, bright red against the bare branches, and Arthur makes sure it's always full of that special seed mix they like. And I sat there watching them, and I knew I should be getting up to start dinner—I had a lovely pot roast planned, with carrots and potatoes, the way my mother used to make it on Sundays—but I just couldn't seem to muster the energy to care about it. I wasn't worried that dinner wouldn't get made, I just felt entirely empty about the whole prospect. 

So, no, not anxious. I don't have that fluttering feeling in my chest or anything like that. I sleep right through the night, mostly, unless Arthur starts snoring, which he does when he sleeps on his back. I just feel so terribly slow and gray inside. Not worried, just... well, just flat, I suppose you could say.
Have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Lost interest? Oh... oh, my, yes. That's exactly it. That's the heart of the matter, really. It's just so strange, Doctor, because I've always been such an active person. Always busy doing something. But lately... well, things I used to absolutely love just sit there, and I can't make myself care about them at all. 

Take my watercolors, for instance. I've painted for years, mostly landscapes and little still lifes. I have a lovely setup in the spare room, right by the window where the light is best in the mornings. I was working on a lovely little piece, a view of the old stone bridge over at the park, but my brushes have just been sitting there drying out for weeks. I look at them, and I know I should pick them up, but the thought of mixing the colors and washing the brushes... it just feels like moving mountains. 

And my tomato plants! Oh, usually by this time of year I'm out there every morning, checking for hornworms, pruning the suckers, making sure the soil is just damp enough. I grow the big heirloom ones, the Brandywine and the Cherokee Purple—they make the most wonderful sandwiches, just a little mayonnaise and salt on toasted sourdough. But this year? I look out the kitchen window at them, and they're getting all overgrown and wild, and I just... I just feel nothing. I can't bring myself to put on my gardening shoes and go out there. 

Even the line dancing! Arthur and I have gone to the senior center for line dancing every Tuesday evening for, oh, it must be five years now. It's such good exercise, and we have such a nice group of friends there. Marge and Harold, and Betty—Betty always brings those little powdered sugar cookies she makes. But the last few weeks, when Tuesday rolls around, I just tell Arthur to go without me. I sit in my armchair and think about them all doing the Electric Slide, and I just don't have the slightest desire to join them. 

And like I was saying before about the cardinals out back... usually I get such a thrill seeing them at the feeder. I used to keep a little notebook by the window to write down when the first one appeared each winter. Now I just look at them and think, "Oh, it's a bird," and that's the end of it. The joy has just... evaporated. It's like someone turned the color down on the television set and everything is just sort of gray and flat. So yes, Doctor, I suppose I have lost interest. Quite a lot of it, I'm afraid.
Have you been feeling worthless lately?

Worthless? Oh... no, no, I don't think so. That's a very strong word, isn't it? Worthless. Let me think about that... 

I mean, I know I'm not doing nearly as much around the house as I usually do, like I was just saying about letting the tomato plants go and not keeping up with my painting, but I certainly don't feel like I have no *worth*. Arthur would be absolutely lost without me, for one thing! Bless his heart, but the man can hardly find his own slippers in the morning without me pointing them out to him. Just yesterday he was turning the hall closet upside down looking for his light windbreaker—the navy blue one we bought at that little shop in Cape May on our anniversary trip three years ago, such a lovely trip that was, we walked on the boardwalk every single morning—anyway, he was making an absolute mess of the closet, and I just had to sigh and tell him it was hanging on the hook by the back door exactly where he left it. So, you see, I'm quite necessary around here. 

And my granddaughter, Emily, the one getting married in California... she called me just the other evening specifically to ask for my recipe for peach cobbler. The one with the lattice crust that I always make for the Fourth of July picnic. She said, "Grammy, nobody makes it like you do, and I want to learn how before the wedding." So, no, I don't feel worthless at all. I know my family loves me and needs me. 

It's just... well, it's just that heavy, gray feeling I mentioned. The fog. It makes me feel terribly *useless* sometimes, in the moment, when I'm just sitting in my chair staring at the wall instead of doing the dusting. The dust on the mantelpiece is getting quite thick, to be perfectly honest with you, and usually I'm an absolute stickler for a clean house. My mother always taught me to keep a tidy parlor in case company called—not that people just drop by unannounced much anymore, which is a shame, really, people used to be so much more neighborly. But being useless at doing my chores for a few weeks isn't the same as being worthless as a human being, is it? I know I still matter to people. I just wish I had the gumption to do the things I ought to be doing for them. So, no, I definitely wouldn't use the word worthless.
Have you been feeling down or sad most days lately?

Sad or down? Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, people always assume if you're not quite yourself, you must be sitting in a corner crying into a handkerchief, but I haven't shed a single tear. When I think of being sad, I think of real sorrow, you know? Like when my dear friend Martha passed away two winters ago. Oh, that was a truly heartbreaking time. Martha and I had been friends since we were girls in high school. We used to walk down to the five-and-dime together every Friday afternoon and share a cherry phosphate, back when things were so much simpler and you could get a treat for a nickel. When she passed, I cried every single day for a month. I couldn't even look at the yellow rose bush she gave me for my fiftieth birthday without tearing up. That is what being sad feels like to me.

But lately? No, it is not that at all. I don't feel like crying. In fact, just the other night, Arthur and I were watching television. He loves those old
Have you had less energy than usual lately?

Less energy? Oh, goodness, yes. It's like my battery is just completely drained, if you know what I mean. 

I go to bed at a reasonable hour, you know. Arthur and I are usually under the covers by ten o'clock, right after the local news—we like the anchorman on channel four, he has such a trustworthy face, not like some of these young kids they put on television nowadays who look like they barely know how to tie their own shoes. And I sleep through the night, I really do. We have a very firm mattress, which the chiropractor told Arthur was best for his lower back, and I'm quite used to it by now. But when I wake up? Oh, I am just so terribly tired. I wake up completely exhausted, even after sleeping the whole night through. It's as if I hadn't slept a wink. 

I pull myself out of bed, and I go to the washroom to wash my face. I've always used cold water and a bit of Pears soap—my mother swore by it for a good complexion, and I've used it my whole life, the translucent amber bars, you know the ones? They smell so beautifully clean. But lately, just standing there at the sink, washing my face and patting it dry... it takes it right out of me. 

Then I go down to the kitchen to make breakfast. Nothing fancy, mind you, just putting the kettle on for tea—Earl Grey for me, Arthur likes his English Breakfast—and making a bit of toast. We buy that nice thick-sliced whole wheat from the bakery down on Main Street, the one with the green awning next to the florist. But by the time I've got the tea steeped and the toast buttered... well, I feel like I need to sit down again. Just doing those few little things, washing up and making a simple breakfast, it completely exhausts me. I have to pull out my chair at the kitchen table and just sit there to recover before I can even think about taking a bite of my toast. I just have absolutely no energy at all, Doctor. It takes everything I have just to get the morning started.
Have you been having trouble concentrating, such as when reading the newspaper or following a television program?

Concentrating? Oh, yes, absolutely. In fact, that's really the main reason I made this appointment to see you in the first place, Doctor. My head just feels... well, foggy is the only word for it. Like it's stuffed with cotton wool. 

I've always prided myself on having a mind like a steel trap, you know. Arthur used to say I was the family calendar, the address book, and the filing cabinet all rolled into one. If he needed to know when the car insurance was due or what size sweater our grandson wore, he just asked me. But lately? Oh, it's just dreadful. I keep mixing up the simplest things. 

Just last week, I was trying to organize the volunteers for the historical society's annual bake sale—we do it every spring to raise money for the museum roof, and I've been the coordinator for twelve years now. Usually, I can keep the whole schedule in my head. But I was looking at my list, and I completely forgot which volunteer I had already called. I ended up calling poor Mrs. Higgins three times in one afternoon to ask if she was bringing her famous lemon bars. Three times! She was very polite about it, of course, she's a lovely woman, her husband used to run the hardware store before they retired, but I felt like an absolute fool. 

And it's not just the phone calls. I've been getting my appointment times completely jumbled up. I showed up for my podiatrist appointment—Dr. Scholl, such a funny name for a foot doctor, isn't it? But he's very gentle with my bunions—anyway, I showed up on a Tuesday when my appointment was actually on Thursday. The receptionist, a very sweet young girl with braces, had to show me the little card she wrote out for me just to prove it. And the exhibit dates at the museum! I told the ladies at my garden club that the new quilt exhibit opened on the 15th, and a whole group of them went down there only to find out it didn't open until the 25th. I was so embarrassed I could hardly look them in the eye at our next meeting. 

So, yes, following a television program or reading the paper is quite difficult right now because my mind just won't hold onto anything. I read a paragraph in the morning paper—we still get the physical paper delivered, Arthur likes to do the crossword puzzle over his coffee—and by the time I get to the end of the page, I've completely forgotten what the article was about. It's just this awful, thick fog in my head, and it's making me feel so terribly muddled all the time.
Have you gotten lost in familiar places?

Lost? Oh, goodness, no. No, I haven't gotten lost. I know this town like the back of my hand, Doctor. Arthur and I have lived in the same house on Elm Street for forty-seven years. It's the pale yellow one with the wrap-around porch and the large oak tree in the front yard—the tree was just a sapling when we moved in, can you believe it? Now its branches reach all the way over the roof. 

So, no, I certainly don't get lost. I drive myself to the grocery store, the pharmacy, the post office—though I must admit, I don't care for the new one-way street they put in downtown by the old library. It used to be a two-way street, and it was perfectly fine for fifty years, but the city council decided they needed to change it to improve traffic flow. Traffic flow! In a town our size! Arthur wrote a very stern letter to the editor of the local paper about it, but of course, it didn't do any good. But even with that silly new traffic pattern, I know exactly where I'm going. 

I take my regular route to the Piggly Wiggly every Tuesday morning—Tuesday is senior discount day, you see, ten percent off your total bill, which really adds up when you're on a fixed income like Arthur and me. I park in the same section of the lot, right near the cart return so I don't have to walk too far with my bags, and I know exactly which aisle has the canned peaches Arthur likes for his cottage cheese. So, no, getting lost isn't a problem at all. It's just my memory that's giving me trouble, like I said, not my sense of direction. My internal compass is still pointing true north, thank heavens.
Have you noticed a change in your appetite lately?

Appetite? Oh, my, yes. Arthur was just saying the other day that I've started eating like a little bird. 

I used to love cooking, you know. I was always in the kitchen. I'd make a lovely pot roast on Sundays with carrots and those little red potatoes, and we'd have leftovers for sandwiches on Monday, and I always made sure we had a proper hot supper every evening. But lately... well, I just don't have the desire for any of it. Food just doesn't sound good to me at all. It's like my taste buds have simply gone to sleep, or my stomach has just decided it's closed for business. 

Most days, I just end up picking at a piece of dry toast or maybe heating up a little bowl of soup. Just a clear broth or maybe some of that Campbell's tomato soup, nothing heavy. And even then, I just sit there and stir it around with my spoon. I can barely manage a few bites before I have to push the bowl away. Arthur gets so worried, bless his heart. He tries to tempt me with those little Scottish shortbread cookies I usually love, the ones that come in the lovely plaid tin, but I just can't bring myself to eat them. I look at them and I just feel entirely indifferent.

And because of it, well, my clothes are just hanging off me. I was getting dressed for church this past Sunday—we go to the First Presbyterian on the corner of Elm and Maple, Reverend Thomas gives such wonderful sermons, though he does tend to go on a bit long sometimes if he gets fired up about the Old Testament—anyway, I put on my good navy blue wool skirt. It's the one with the pleats that I bought at Macy's a few years ago, a very classic cut. And it was just swimming on me! My skirts have gotten so terribly loose I had to take a large safety pin to the waistband just to keep it from slipping right down my hips. And it's not just that one, it's all my everyday skirts, too. I certainly haven't been trying to lose weight, Doctor, goodness knows at my age you don't go on silly diets, but the weight is just falling off anyway because I simply can't bring myself to eat a proper meal.
Have you lost weight lately without trying?

Well, yes, Doctor, exactly like I was just saying! I haven't been trying to lose a single pound. Goodness, at my age, you don't go on silly diets, you just want to enjoy your meals and be comfortable. But just like I mentioned with that navy blue skirt... all of my clothes have gotten so terribly loose. 

I actually had Arthur bring the bathroom scale out into the hallway just yesterday morning—it's one of those heavy old metal ones we bought at Sears Roebuck decades ago, the kind with the little dial that spins around, much more reliable than these new digital things that always seem to need a new battery right when you want to use them. Anyway, I stepped on it, and I was just shocked at where the needle stopped. The weight is just falling right off me without me doing a single thing to make it happen. 

But I suppose it makes perfect sense when you think about it. When you spend most days just picking at a piece of dry toast or staring at a little bowl of soup because food simply doesn't sound good anymore... well, the pounds are bound to just slip away, aren't they? If this keeps up, I'm going to have to take half my wardrobe down to Maria—she's the seamstress over on 4th Street, she does wonderful work with hems and alterations, her mother used to run the shop before her—just to have all my waistbands taken in. Have you ever been told that your vitamin B12 level was low?

Vitamin B12? Oh, let me think... no, I don't believe so. I don't think anyone has ever mentioned that to me. 

Now, Dr. Peterson—he was my primary care doctor for thirty years, wonderful man, always wore those lovely patterned bow ties, though he retired a few years ago to spend time with his grandchildren in Florida—he always used to say my bloodwork was boring, which he said was the very best kind of bloodwork to have. He'd run all those tests every year at my annual checkup, you know, they draw it right there in the office. The nurse, Betty, she had the gentlest touch, never left a bruise. I've always had veins that roll, they call it, so sometimes it takes them a try or two, but Betty always got it on the first try. 

Anyway, Dr. Peterson would send it off to the lab, and then a week later he'd call and say everything was right where it ought to be. My new doctor, Dr. Evans, she's very thorough too, very modern office, everything is on a computer now instead of those thick paper charts Dr. Peterson had. She ran a whole panel of tests just a few months ago when I went in for my checkup, and she didn't say a word about any vitamins being low. I do take a little daily multivitamin, one of those Centrum Silver ones for women over fifty, the little purple pill. Arthur takes the men's version, the gray one. We get them at the Costco because it's so much cheaper to buy the big double pack, even if it takes us a year to get through them. I take it every morning right after breakfast, with a small glass of orange juice—the kind with no pulp, Arthur can't stand pulp. But as for a doctor actually telling me my B12 was low, no, I've never heard that. Everything has always been perfectly normal in that department, thank goodness.

But I just sat there looking at the phone, feeling completely overwhelmed by the steps. I couldn't hold the information in my head long enough to make a decision. Well, it certainly wasn't overnight, if that's what you mean. It wasn't like waking up one morning and suddenly my brain was full of cotton wool. No, it's been more of a... a creeping thing, I suppose you could say. It really all started about four months ago. I remember the timing quite clearly because that was right around when we had that dreadful water damage in the downstairs bathroom. Oh, what a nightmare that was! The pipe under the sink just burst right in the middle of the night, and by the time Arthur heard the dripping, the water had seeped all the way out into the hallway carpet. 

We had to rip up the flooring, and of course, once you start pulling things apart in a house as old as ours, you find all sorts of other issues, so we ended up having to do a whole remodel. And I tell you, dealing with the contractors, picking out new tile, trying to keep the dust out of the rest of the house... it was chaotic. And that's really when I first started noticing that I wasn't quite myself. At first, I just thought I was distracted by all the noise and the mess. I'd misplace the contractor's estimate or forget to call the plumber back when I said I would, and I just chalked it up to the stress of having our home turned upside down. 

But then the remodel finished up—oh, about two months ago now, and the new tile really is lovely, a sort of seafoam green, very calming—but the fogginess didn't go away. In fact, it just seemed to settle in deeper. So, yes, it's been about four months in total, gradually getting to this point where I'm missing appointments and mixing up the heritage center calendar. Well, you know, I've thought about that quite a bit actually, because Arthur asked me the very same thing just the other day when I couldn't remember where I put the new box of Earl Grey. I was standing right there in the kitchen, and he said, "Margaret, is it worse right now, or is it always like this?" And I had to stop and really consider it. 

I suppose... I suppose it’s pretty much the same all the time. It doesn't seem to matter if it's first thing in the morning when I'm having my toast and marmalade, or late in the afternoon when I'm trying to read the paper. The fog is just... there. It’s a constant sort of thickness. I mean, there are moments, of course, where I might feel a tiny bit clearer, maybe just after a good cup of tea, but it's not like the confusion suddenly lifts like a curtain and then drops back down again. It's not a coming-and-going sort of thing at all. 

It’s just a steady, unrelenting muddle. Like trying to look through a smudged window that you can never quite wipe clean, no matter what time of day it is. I remember my Aunt Clara—she lived to be ninety-two, bless her—she used to get very confused, but only in the evenings. They call it "sundowning," I think? The nurses at her care home told us about it. She’d be perfectly sharp at lunch, telling us all the town gossip, and then by dinner time, she wouldn't know what decade it was. But I'm not like Aunt Clara. For me, it's just this constant, low-level haze from the moment I wake up until I go to sleep. It never really gives me a break, which is partly why it’s so terribly exhausting, I think.

The whole idea just floats away. But it's not that I'm grasping for a specific word, like a noun or a verb that's on the tip of my tongue. It's not like I'm looking at a... a spoon and calling it a shovel, or anything silly like that. My vocabulary is perfectly fine, thank heavens. 

I've always prided myself on being quite articulate, actually. I used to win spelling bees when I was a girl, you know. I even won the county championship in 1958 with the word "chrysanthemum." So, no, the words themselves are all still up there, tucked away where they belong. It's just the overarching thought that gets muddled in all that cotton wool I mentioned. I just sort of trail off because I forget where the sentence was supposed to end up! But finding the actual words? No, I wouldn't say I've had any trouble with that at all, just the general confusion of it all.

Arthur is constantly fiddling with the thermostat. He’ll sneak it up to 72 degrees when I’m not looking, and I have to go right behind him and turn it back down to 68 because otherwise it feels like an absolute sauna in the front sitting room! 

Just yesterday, he was sitting in his recliner with that heavy wool blanket—the green tartan one we brought back from our trip to Scotland in, oh, it must have been 1998—wrapped right up to his chin, asking if I didn't feel a chill. And I was sitting right there in just a light cotton blouse, perfectly comfortable. 

You know, they always keep the grocery store absolutely freezing, too, especially down the dairy aisle where they keep the milk and the butter. I was just there on Tuesday getting some double cream for a recipe, and even there, I haven't felt the need to wear anything more than my usual light cardigan. So, no, I haven't been feeling unusually cold at all. My internal thermometer seems to be working just exactly as it always has, thank goodness. It's really just my thoughts that are all jumbled up in that fog I was telling you about, not my temperature!

Arthur bought it for me at the pharmacy down the street, the one next to the bakery that makes those wonderful lemon tarts. He said, "Margaret, this will help keep things straight," and he was right, it really does. I sit down every Sunday evening after dinner and sort them all out for the week. 

But as for anything *new*... well, I've been on my usual blood pressure pill for years now, the little white one, and my cholesterol medication, which is sort of an oval shape. Dr. Henderson—he was my primary care doctor before he retired last spring, lovely man, always asked after my garden—he started me on those ages ago. And I take my daily vitamin, of course. 

But anything in the last few months? No, I really don't think so. I haven't been to the pharmacy for anything new, just the regular refills. Arthur usually picks them up for me when he goes to get the Sunday paper. So, no, nothing new at all. Just the same old routine. It's just this... this awful fog that seems to have rolled in all on its own, without any new pills to blame it on!

Numbness or tingling? In my hands or feet? Oh, goodness, let me think about that for a second... No, I really don't think so. My hands and feet feel just the way they always do. 

I mean, sometimes if I sit with my legs crossed too long—like when I'm reading in my armchair by the front window, the one where the afternoon sun comes in so nicely, I was just reading that new biography of Eleanor Roosevelt there yesterday, fascinating woman, truly ahead of her time—if I sit like that for an hour or two, my foot might fall asleep. You know that pins-and-needles feeling when you stand up? But that's just normal, isn't it? Everyone gets that. You just shake it out and stamp your foot a few times on the rug and it goes right away. 

And my hands... well, Arthur always says my hands are as steady as a rock. I still do all my own needlepoint, you know. I'm working on a lovely floral piece right now for my granddaughter's wedding present—she's getting married in September, out in California, which is a terribly long flight, but we wouldn't miss it for the world. It's a pattern of hydrangeas and tea roses, very intricate, lots of tiny stitches. If my hands were numb or tingling, I could never manage the needle, could I? I'd be dropping it constantly or pricking my fingers, and I haven't done that at all. 

I do wear my gardening gloves when I'm out in the yard, of course, the thick leather ones, because the rosebushes can be so unforgiving if you're not careful. But underneath the gloves, my hands feel perfectly fine. I can feel the soil and the stems and everything just as clear as a bell. So no, no strange tingling or numbness anywhere. patient.answer:
Anxious or worried? Oh, well... I wouldn't say I've been anxious, exactly. Not worried in the sense of wringing my hands or pacing the floors. I mean, Arthur worries enough for the both of us, quite frankly. He's always fretting about the gutters needing cleaning or whether the car's oil needs changing, even though he just took it in last month to that nice young mechanic down on Elm Street—the one whose mother used to run the florist shop before it closed. 

But for me? No, I don't feel that sort of nervous worry. It's more just... well, this awful fog I keep mentioning. It's so heavy, you see. It just sits there, pressing down on everything. I don't feel anxious about it, I just feel... stuck in it. Like trying to walk through molasses. 

Just the other day, I was sitting at the kitchen table, looking out at the bird feeder. We get the loveliest cardinals this time of year, bright red against the bare branches, and Arthur makes sure it's always full of that special seed mix they like. And I sat there watching them, and I knew I should be getting up to start dinner—I had a lovely pot roast planned, with carrots and potatoes, the way my mother used to make it on Sundays—but I just couldn't seem to muster the energy to care about it. I wasn't worried that dinner wouldn't get made, I just felt entirely empty about the whole prospect. 

So, no, not anxious. I don't have that fluttering feeling in my chest or anything like that. I sleep right through the night, mostly, unless Arthur starts snoring, which he does when he sleeps on his back. I just feel so terribly slow and gray inside. Not worried, just... well, just flat, I suppose you could say.

patient.answer:
Lost interest? Oh... oh, my, yes. That's exactly it. That's the heart of the matter, really. It's just so strange, Doctor, because I've always been such an active person. Always busy doing something. But lately... well, things I used to absolutely love just sit there, and I can't make myself care about them at all. 

Take my watercolors, for instance. I've painted for years, mostly landscapes and little still lifes. I have a lovely setup in the spare room, right by the window where the light is best in the mornings. I was working on a lovely little piece, a view of the old stone bridge over at the park, but my brushes have just been sitting there drying out for weeks. I look at them, and I know I should pick them up, but the thought of mixing the colors and washing the brushes... it just feels like moving mountains. 

And my tomato plants! Oh, usually by this time of year I'm out there every morning, checking for hornworms, pruning the suckers, making sure the soil is just damp enough. I grow the big heirloom ones, the Brandywine and the Cherokee Purple—they make the most wonderful sandwiches, just a little mayonnaise and salt on toasted sourdough. But this year? I look out the kitchen window at them, and they're getting all overgrown and wild, and I just... I just feel nothing. I can't bring myself to put on my gardening shoes and go out there. 

Even the line dancing! Arthur and I have gone to the senior center for line dancing every Tuesday evening for, oh, it must be five years now. It's such good exercise, and we have such a nice group of friends there. Marge and Harold, and Betty—Betty always brings those little powdered sugar cookies she makes. But the last few weeks, when Tuesday rolls around, I just tell Arthur to go without me. I sit in my armchair and think about them all doing the Electric Slide, and I just don't have the slightest desire to join them. 

And like I was saying before about the cardinals out back... usually I get such a thrill seeing them at the feeder. I used to keep a little notebook by the window to write down when the first one appeared each winter. Now I just look at them and think, "Oh, it's a bird," and that's the end of it. The joy has just... evaporated. It's like someone turned the color down on the television set and everything is just sort of gray and flat. So yes, Doctor, I suppose I have lost interest. Quite a lot of it, I'm afraid.

doctor.question: Have you had less energy than usual lately?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: I wake up tired even after sleeping, and by the time I wash up and make breakfast I feel like I need to sit down again.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about having less energy than usual, which directly maps to the Fatigue symptom.

Less energy? Oh, goodness, yes. It's like my battery is just completely drained, if you know what I mean. 

I go to bed at a reasonable hour, you know. Arthur and I are usually under the covers by ten o'clock, right after the local news—we like the anchorman on channel four, he has such a trustworthy face, not like some of these young kids they put on television nowadays who look like they barely know how to tie their own shoes. And I sleep through the night, I really do. We have a very firm mattress, which the chiropractor told Arthur was best for his lower back, and I'm quite used to it by now. But when I wake up? Oh, I am just so terribly tired. I wake up completely exhausted, even after sleeping the whole night through. It's as if I hadn't slept a wink. 

I pull myself out of bed, and I go to the washroom to wash my face. I've always used cold water and a bit of Pears soap—my mother swore by it for a good complexion, and I've used it my whole life, the translucent amber bars, you know the ones? They smell so beautifully clean. But lately, just standing there at the sink, washing my face and patting it dry... it takes it right out of me.

We buy that nice thick-sliced whole wheat from the bakery down on Main Street, the one with the green awning next to the florist. But by the time I've got the tea steeped and the toast buttered... well, I feel like I need to sit down again. Just doing those few little things, washing up and making a simple breakfast, it completely exhausts me. I have to pull out my chair at the kitchen table and just sit there to recover before I can even think about taking a bite of my toast. I just have absolutely no energy at all, Doctor. It takes everything I have just to get the morning started.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the current syndrome includes impaired concentration/indecisiveness as part of a depressive episode versus a primary neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble concentrating, such as when reading the newspaper or following a television program?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that my head feels foggy and I keep mixing up simple things, like appointment times, exhibit dates, and which volunteer I already called.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble concentrating, which directly maps to the Diminished_Thinking symptom where the patient experiences a foggy head and mixes up simple things.

patient.answer:
Concentrating? Oh, yes, absolutely. In fact, that's really the main reason I made this appointment to see you in the first place, Doctor. My head just feels... well, foggy is the only word for it. Like it's stuffed with cotton wool. 

I've always prided myself on having a mind like a steel trap, you know. Arthur used to say I was the family calendar, the address book, and the filing cabinet all rolled into one. If he needed to know when the car insurance was due or what size sweater our grandson wore, he just asked me. But lately? Oh, it's just dreadful. I keep mixing up the simplest things. 

Just last week, I was trying to organize the volunteers for the historical society's annual bake sale—we do it every spring to raise money for the museum roof, and I've been the coordinator for twelve years now. Usually, I can keep the whole schedule in my head. But I was looking at my list, and I completely forgot which volunteer I had already called. I ended up calling poor Mrs. Higgins three times in one afternoon to ask if she was bringing her famous lemon bars. Three times! She was very polite about it, of course, she's a lovely woman, her husband used to run the hardware store before they retired, but I felt like an absolute fool. 

And it's not just the phone calls. I've been getting my appointment times completely jumbled up. I showed up for my podiatrist appointment—Dr. Scholl, such a funny name for a foot doctor, isn't it? But he's very gentle with my bunions—anyway, I showed up on a Tuesday when my appointment was actually on Thursday. The receptionist, a very sweet young girl with braces, had to show me the little card she wrote out for me just to prove it. And the exhibit dates at the museum! I told the ladies at my garden club that the new quilt exhibit opened on the 15th, and a whole group of them went down there only to find out it didn't open until the 25th. I was so embarrassed I could hardly look them in the eye at our next meeting. 

So, yes, following a television program or reading the paper is quite difficult right now because my mind just won't hold onto anything. I read a paragraph in the morning paper—we still get the physical paper delivered, Arthur likes to do the crossword puzzle over his coffee—and by the time I get to the end of the page, I've completely forgotten what the article was about. It's just this awful, thick fog in my head, and it's making me feel so terribly muddled all the time.

Lost? Oh, goodness, no. No, I haven't gotten lost. I know this town like the back of my hand, Doctor. Arthur and I have lived in the same house on Elm Street for forty-seven years. It's the pale yellow one with the wrap-around porch and the large oak tree in the front yard—the tree was just a sapling when we moved in, can you believe it? Now its branches reach all the way over the roof. 

So, no, I certainly don't get lost. I drive myself to the grocery store, the pharmacy, the post office—though I must admit, I don't care for the new one-way street they put in downtown by the old library. It used to be a two-way street, and it was perfectly fine for fifty years, but the city council decided they needed to change it to improve traffic flow. Traffic flow! In a town our size! Arthur wrote a very stern letter to the editor of the local paper about it, but of course, it didn't do any good. But even with that silly new traffic pattern, I know exactly where I'm going. 

I take my regular route to the Piggly Wiggly every Tuesday morning—Tuesday is senior discount day, you see, ten percent off your total bill, which really adds up when you're on a fixed income like Arthur and me. I park in the same section of the lot, right near the cart return so I don't have to walk too far with my bags, and I know exactly which aisle has the canned peaches Arthur likes for his cottage cheese. So, no, getting lost isn't a problem at all. It's just my memory that's giving me trouble, like I said, not my sense of direction. My internal compass is still pointing true north, thank heavens.

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: Most days I pick at toast or soup because food doesn't sound good, and my skirts have gotten loose without me trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite, which directly corresponds to the Weight_Appetite_Change symptom.

patient.answer:
Appetite? Oh, my, yes. Arthur was just saying the other day that I've started eating like a little bird. 

I used to love cooking, you know. I was always in the kitchen. I'd make a lovely pot roast on Sundays with carrots and those little red potatoes, and we'd have leftovers for sandwiches on Monday, and I always made sure we had a proper hot supper every evening. But lately... well, I just don't have the desire for any of it. Food just doesn't sound good to me at all. It's like my taste buds have simply gone to sleep, or my stomach has just decided it's closed for business. 

Most days, I just end up picking at a piece of dry toast or maybe heating up a little bowl of soup. Just a clear broth or maybe some of that Campbell's tomato soup, nothing heavy. And even then, I just sit there and stir it around with my spoon. I can barely manage a few bites before I have to push the bowl away. Arthur gets so worried, bless his heart. He tries to tempt me with those little Scottish shortbread cookies I usually love, the ones that come in the lovely plaid tin, but I just can't bring myself to eat them. I look at them and I just feel entirely indifferent.

And because of it, well, my clothes are just hanging off me. I was getting dressed for church this past Sunday—we go to the First Presbyterian on the corner of Elm and Maple, Reverend Thomas gives such wonderful sermons, though he does tend to go on a bit long sometimes if he gets fired up about the Old Testament—anyway, I put on my good navy blue wool skirt. It's the one with the pleats that I bought at Macy's a few years ago, a very classic cut. And it was just swimming on me! My skirts have gotten so terribly loose I had to take a large safety pin to the waistband just to keep it from slipping right down my hips. And it's not just that one, it's all my everyday skirts, too. I certainly haven't been trying to lose weight, Doctor, goodness knows at my age you don't go on silly diets, but the weight is just falling off anyway because I simply can't bring myself to eat a proper meal.

Vitamin B12? Oh, let me think... no, I don't believe so. I don't think anyone has ever mentioned that to me. 

Now, Dr. Peterson—he was my primary care doctor for thirty years, wonderful man, always wore those lovely patterned bow ties, though he retired a few years ago to spend time with his grandchildren in Florida—he always used to say my bloodwork was boring, which he said was the very best kind of bloodwork to have. He'd run all those tests every year at my annual checkup, you know, they draw it right there in the office. The nurse, Betty, she had the gentlest touch, never left a bruise. I've always had veins that roll, they call it, so sometimes it takes them a try or two, but Betty always got it on the first try. 

Anyway, Dr. Peterson would send it off to the lab, and then a week later he'd call and say everything was right where it ought to be. My iron was always good, my cholesterol was fine—well, maybe a tiny bit high once, but then Arthur and I switched from whole milk to two percent for our morning oatmeal and it went right back down. My new doctor, Dr. Evans, she's very thorough too, very modern office, everything is on a computer now instead of those thick paper charts Dr. Peterson had. She ran a whole panel of tests just a few months ago when I went in for my checkup, and she didn't say a word about any vitamins being low. I do take a little daily multivitamin, one of those Centrum Silver ones for women over fifty, the little purple pill. Arthur takes the men's version, the gray one. We get them at the Costco because it's so much cheaper to buy the big double pack, even if it takes us a year to get through them. I take it every morning right after breakfast, with a small glass of orange juice—the kind with no pulp, Arthur can't stand pulp. But as for a doctor actually telling me my B12 was low, no, I've never heard that. Everything has always been perfectly normal in that department, thank goodness.
